description_full: General Electric Company, doing business as GE Aerospace, designs and produces commercial and defense aircraft engines, integrated engine components, electric power, and aircraft systems. The company operates through two segments, Commercial Engines & Services, and Defense & Propulsion Technologies. The Commercial Engines & Services segment designs, develops, manufactures, maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) services of jet engines and sale of spare parts for commercial airframes, business aviation, and aeroderivative applications. The Defense & Propulsion Technologies designs, develops, manufactures, and services jet engines and avionics and power systems for governments, militaries, and commercial airframers, as well as MRO of engines and the sale of spare parts. This segment also offers aircraft components and systems, such as small turboprop engines, aeroengine mechanical transmissions, turbines, combustors and controls, additive manufacturing, propeller systems, ignition systems, sensors and engine accessories for fixed wing and rotorcraft applications for commercial and military end users under the Avio Aero, Unison, Dowty Propellers, and Colibrium Additive brands. The company operates in the United States, Europe, Asia, the Americas, the Middle East, and Africa. General Electric Company was incorporated in 1892 and is based in Evendale, Ohio.

financial_summary: GE Aerospace is a mega-cap industrials business with a $342.9B market cap on $45.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -16% over the past three years and -9% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 17% against a 10% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $7.3B in free cash flow — roughly 16 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.98× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.7× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 12× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.1× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 211% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 2 other valuation measures)
Revenue growth in the bottom decile of Industrials peers — losing share inside the profit pool
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $14.8M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Industrials sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 6% over 3 months
Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sector_tailwinds: Operating margins 15% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
64 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment

sect: Its 24% operating margin runs 15pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.13x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 1.2% of sector revenue and 2.5% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-5.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 15% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 35% and a beta of 1.12, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $1.4B traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 58% in the 2020 crash, 41% in the 2022 bear market and 81% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $107 (margin of safety -211%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 35%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $74.38 to $153 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 37.9 vs 24.1, EV/EBITDA 30.4 vs 13.4 and P/FCF 47.2 vs 22.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 100% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.1% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 21 covering analysts target $378 on average, 14% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 17% clears the cost of capital of 9.8% by 7pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.70).
It converts 16% of revenue into free cash flow.
ROE of 47% is amplified by 7.0x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
Operating margin is running 17pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 3.4% of revenue on R&D and 0.7% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.7x net debt to EBITDA ($9.8B of cash against $20.5B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 12.3x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -15.7% over 3 years, -10.4% over 5 years and -9.0% over 10 years, so the decline is deepening, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 14%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 83.9% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.41 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 4.2x annual revenue and deferred revenue up 10%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.5x, 2.8% of sales), a maintenance pace.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and institutions hold 81%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (12 sales, net $14.8M sold).
It returns 2.8% a year to shareholders (2.2% in buybacks and 0.6% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.2% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 64 consecutive years.
people: With about 57,000 employees, each generates about $804K of revenue, 2.2x the Industrials median, and revenue has fallen 7.4% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $127K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $10.3M (13x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
